cards.front: What is the difference between an element and a compound?
cards.back: An **element** contains only one type of atom. A **compound** contains atoms of two or more different elements that are chemically bonded together.
cards.hint: Count how many types of atom are in each substance.

cards.front: Why does an atom have no overall charge?
cards.back: It has equal numbers of **protons** (positive) and **electrons** (negative), so their charges cancel out.
cards.hint: Compare the charges of the particles in the nucleus with those in the shells.

cards.front: What makes two atoms belong to the same element?
cards.back: They have the same number of **protons**. An element contains only atoms with the same number of protons.

cards.front: What is the nucleus of an atom?
cards.back: The small central region containing **protons** and **neutrons**. Almost all of the atom's mass is in the nucleus.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to draw electrons mixed in with the protons and neutrons in an atom?
cards.back: Electrons occupy **shells** outside the nucleus, so they should be drawn outside it, not with the protons and neutrons.

cards.front: How should a chemical symbol be written?
cards.back: It starts with a **capital letter**. Any second letter is lower case, so helium is $\text{He}$, not $\text{HE}$.

cards.front: Why does $\text{O}_2$ not count as a compound even though its two atoms are bonded?
cards.back: Both atoms are **oxygen**, so it contains only one element. A compound needs two or more different elements.
cards.hint: Look at how many types of atom it contains.

cards.front: What do the numbers in the formula $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ tell you?
cards.back: The number after each symbol gives how many atoms of that element are in each group. So each water molecule has **two** hydrogen atoms and **one** oxygen atom.
cards.hint: Read the small number written after each element symbol.

cards.front: How can you tell from a formula whether a substance is an element or a compound?
cards.back: One element symbol, even with a small number, means an **element**. More than one symbol means a **compound**. So $\text{Fe}$ is an element and $\text{FeS}$ is a compound.
cards.hint: Count the element symbols, not the numbers.

cards.front: Why can't filtering separate the atoms in a compound?
cards.back: The atoms are **chemically bonded**, and physical methods such as filtering cannot break those bonds.
cards.hint: Think about what holds the atoms together.

cards.front: What does a particle diagram show?
cards.back: Atoms drawn as **circles**. Touching circles in a group show bonded atoms, and separate groups show separate particles.

cards.front: How do you draw a particle diagram of pure water?
cards.back: 1. Draw one **oxygen** circle touching two hydrogen circles to form a group. 2. Repeat the same separate group to show a sample of pure water.
cards.hint: Start with the smallest bonded unit in water.

cards.front: What does a particle diagram show when different particles appear without all being bonded into the same groups?
cards.back: It shows a **mixture**, not a compound.

cards.front: Why can't you assume two neighbouring atoms in a particle diagram are bonded?
cards.back: Atoms near each other are not necessarily bonded. Show a **bond** by joining or touching their circles.
